newsitem.title: USA: Beijing denies complicity in U.S. campaign scandal.
newsitem.headline: Beijing denies complicity in U.S. campaign scandal.

text.p: Chinese vice premier Zhu Rongji denied any Chinese complicity in the U.S. election campaign finance scandal, Newsweek magazine reported on Sunday.
He also dismissed a Newsweek report that China had put $1 million into America's political process through its consulates and embassy in the United States.

"Of course, I think this is totally untrue," Zhu told Newsweek in an exclusive interview in Beijing. "This matter has been played up so much due to the political needs of some people in the United States. It has nothing to do with China."

"On the question of (whether China made improper political contributions to U.S. politicians), if you say Taiwan made them, I might believe it," he said. "But if you say China took part there is no basis in fact.
"Some friends advise us to do lobbying in the United States. But we have principles. I don't think we can learn from Taiwan in this regard," he said.

The Washington Post reported last month that the FBI had intercepts of communications between Beijing and the Chinese Embassy in Washington showing there was a scheme to try to buy influence with U.S. politicians and that it was "government sanctioned."

The allegations of Chinese efforts to buy U.S. political influence by funneling cash into the 1996 presidential and congressional election campaigns -- which if true would be illegal -- are the subject of several probes.
President Clinton's Democratic Party has returned nearly $3 million of questionable donations to campaign contributors, many of them individuals with ties to Asian business interests or governments.

Zhu also maintained that Wang Jung, chairman of China International Trust and Investment Corporation, who has been depicted as an arms dealer and implicated as an alleged donor, had done nothing wrong.

"I once asked him 'Have you made such contributions?' And he said 'I have no money!' I said, If you really have done such things I will dismiss you from the company. He said 'I pledge on my personal integrity I have never done such things'."
Zhu, credited with China's rapid economic growth, also said China's possible future as an economic superpower would not lead to confrontation with the United States.
"China will never get involved in aggression against other countries' internal affairs."
He said trends showed China would maintain eight to 10 percent GDP growth, and inflation at less than five percent until the next century.
